content: CCR10, also known as C-C chemokine receptor type 10, is a protein encoded by the CCR10 gene in humans. Chemokines are a class of small proteins, typically ranging from 8 to 14 kilodaltons in size, that are predominantly basic in nature and share structural similarities. These molecules are critical in regulating the trafficking of various leukocyte subsets by interacting with specific seven-transmembrane, G protein-coupled receptors. In addition to their role in cell trafficking, chemokines are essential for the development, maintenance of homeostasis, and overall function of the immune system. They also exert effects on cells within the central nervous system and endothelial cells, particularly those involved in processes such as angiogenesis (the formation of new blood vessels) or angiostasis (the inhibition of blood vessel formation). Chemokines are categorized into two primary subfamilies, CXCL and CCL, based on the arrangement of the first two conserved cysteine residues out of a total of four. In CXCL chemokines, the two cysteine residues are separated by a single amino acid, whereas in CCL chemokines, the two cysteines are adjacent to one another. CCR10 is a chemokine receptor that specifically binds to the ligands CCL27 and CCL28. This receptor is typically expressed by melanocytes, plasma cells, and skin-homing T cells. Experimental studies have demonstrated that the transduction of CCR10 into B16 melanoma cells significantly enhances the development of lymph node metastases in mice following inoculation into the skin. This finding suggests that CCR10 plays a role in directing metastatic processes. Furthermore, interactions between CCR10 and its ligand CCL27 are implicated in T cell-mediated inflammatory responses in the skin.
